analysis.one_liner: Restores the IRS's ability to enforce the ban on political endorsements by churches and charities.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 31, 2025 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has received no further action, with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Each year's spending law includes a rider that bars the IRS from using funds to enforce the rule against churches and other tax-exempt charities endorsing or opposing candidates for office. This bill would suspend that rider for fiscal year 2025, letting the IRS enforce the rule again. Backers frame this as curbing 'dark money' by keeping political campaign activity out of tax-exempt organizations, whose donors are often hidden.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters benefit if political campaigning is kept out of tax-exempt organizations, whose donors can remain anonymous and whose political costs are effectively subsidized by their tax exemption. Charities and churches that stay out of politics also benefit, since a renewed enforcement rule protects them from pressure to become campaign vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and apolitical churches and charities

how_it_helps.text: The bill suspends the rider in Section 123 of the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act, 2024, which has 'no force or effect' for fiscal year 2025, ending the ban on IRS enforcement of political-activity rules for certain nonprofits [S2].

Restoring enforcement means churches and 501(c)(3) charities that endorse or oppose candidates risk losing tax-exempt treatment, so money funneled through those organizations for elections becomes riskier again [S2].
The bill is titled the End Dark Money Act, reflecting its stated purpose of bringing transparency to the political activity of certain nonprofit organizations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Churches and religious organizations that want to endorse or oppose candidates from the pulpit or in official communications bear the cost, facing IRS enforcement after years of the rule going unenforced. Politically active charities and the donors who fund electioneering through tax-exempt entities also lose a low-risk channel.

drawbacks.text: Restored enforcement restricts speech by churches and charities: organizations that want to weigh in on elections would face losing their tax exemption, and critics argue this chills religious leaders' speech, which is why Congress put the non-enforcement rider into appropriations law in the first place [S2].

The fix is narrow and temporary: it only suspends the restriction for fiscal year 2025, so the non-enforcement rider would have to be stripped from every future spending bill for enforcement to continue, and a single appropriations cycle could restore the status quo [S2].

Any IRS enforcement of political activity rules against churches revives the fear, repeatedly cited in the debate over this rider, that tax authorities could be used against religious or charitable groups for their political views.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For voters who want election spending out of tax-exempt entities, the benefit is real but modest: the underlying rule is already law, so the bill only removes Congress's annual handcuff on the IRS for one year. The cost falls on organizations whose political speech would become legally risky again. The deeper weakness is design — a one-year suspension does not settle the question, so even if enacted it would have to be renewed annually.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 31, 2025 and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has not taken it up, and it has just two cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Jason Crow introduced the End Dark Money Act in the House on March 31, 2025 [S1] [S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, and no further action appears in the record [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats [S3].

The bill would make Section 123 of the 2024 Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act — the rider blocking IRS enforcement of political-activity rules for certain nonprofits — have no force or effect in fiscal year 2025 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the status quo holds: the IRS continues to be barred from enforcing the political-activity rule against tax-exempt organizations, and politically active nonprofits and their donors keep an enforcement-free channel that apolitical taxpayers help subsidize.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo backers in tax-exempt politics

for.name: Rep. Jason Crow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Dark Money Act and referred it to Ways and Means.

for.name: Rep. Nikema Williams
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, has not scheduled a markup or other committee action since the referral in March 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors are House Democrats, and the committee with the bill has taken no action under Republican control.

industries.note: Restored IRS enforcement would again put churches' tax exemption at risk if they endorse or oppose candidates. Supporters argue this protects congregations from being turned into campaign tools; critics see it as a government restriction on religious leaders' speech.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt charities and politically active nonprofits (501(c)(3)s)
industries.note: Organizations could no longer engage in candidate politics without risking their exemption, closing a channel where political money can move without disclosure. Legitimate charities that stay out of elections lose nothing.

industries.industry: Anonymous political donors and campaign operatives
industries.note: Routing election activity through tax-exempt nonprofits becomes riskier again, reducing a low-exposure channel for election spending. Their loss is the transparency gain the bill's title describes.

analysis.trajectory: With only two cosponsors, no committee action since the March 2025 referral, and a Ways and Means committee focused elsewhere, the bill is likely to sit without a markup and expire at the end of this Congress unless it picks up substantial additional support.
